changelog.change: Initial entry — the non-algorithm half of running an arrest: claiming leadership, role assignment, closed-loop comms, CPR-quality targets, epinephrine timing, the calcium/bicarbonate 'leave it in the drawer' evidence, and the refractory-VF practical move. Companion to the Adult Cardiac Arrest algorithm card.

summary: The single biggest determinant of survival is CPR quality, not the drugs. The leader's job is to stand at the foot of the bed and think — not do compressions, not push meds — while assigning every task by name and diagnosing why the patient arrested. Calm is competence; if an order wasn't repeated back, it wasn't heard.

items: Someone leads, out loud, immediately: "I am leading this code."
The leader does not do compressions and does not push meds — the leader thinks. Stand at the foot of the bed, be visible, calm on the surface.
Highest-survival IHCA systems use a pit-crew model: structured roles running in parallel, not sequentially.

body.text: Assign roles — eye contact, name, task

"Sarah, compressions. Mike, airway. Jen, med cart and timer. Alex, recorder. David, you swap in for compressions in 2 minutes. Chris and Maria, runners — stay right outside the door." To everyone else: "Thank you for being here. We have enough hands — rotate in for compressions or please step out." Too many people is chaos; anyone not assigned either gets a job or leaves.

items: Order → read-back → completion. Leader: "Give 1 mg epi IV push." Nurse: "1 mg epi IV push — given." If nobody repeats it back, it didn't happen.
The best-run codes are quiet. No side conversations. An idea gets walked over and said at normal volume; the leader announces the plan. Air-traffic-control tower, not a stadium.

body.text: Chaos is not the same as effort. Calm is competence.
CPR quality is the whole game

items: Rate 100–120/min.
Depth at least 5 cm and under 6 cm — there is a ceiling.
Full chest recoil between compressions.
Chest compression fraction ≥ 60%, aim ≥ 80% — minimise every pause, keep rhythm checks < 10 s.
Swap compressors every 2 minutes: measured depth starts declining around 90 seconds, before the compressor feels tired.
Lower the bed, put a backboard underneath — compressions on a mattress are compressions on a waterbed. Use a real-time feedback device if you have one.

rows: Give epinephrine early — earlier epi tracks with better ROSC across the evidence
Defibrillation first; epinephrine after the initial shocks fail

body.text: 1 mg IV/IO every 3–5 min (about every other CPR cycle). A PARAMEDIC2 post-hoc analysis found epinephrine's benefit over placebo converges toward zero at roughly 20 minutes of pulselessness — early epi matters because the window closes. High-dose epinephrine has no survival benefit in randomised trials.
Calcium and bicarbonate — the sacred cows

items: Calcium (COCA, JAMA 2021): stopped early for a signal of harm — ROSC 19% vs 27% placebo. Routine calcium is NOT recommended (2023 AHA focused update, 2025 AHA). Reserve for confirmed hyperkalaemia or calcium-channel-blocker overdose.

Sodium bicarbonate (BIHCA, JAMA 2026 — first purpose-built RCT in IHCA, 779 patients): sustained ROSC 39% vs 37%, no significant difference in survival or neurologic outcome. Reserve for hyperkalaemia, tricyclic overdose, or known severe metabolic acidosis.
No specific indication → leave both in the drawer.

Amiodarone and lidocaine are treated as equivalent options (2025 AHA) for shock-refractory VF/pVT. Pick one, give it early, move on — the window is narrow and time-dependent (amiodarone within ~8 min of ALS arrival improved discharge survival and function in ALPS subgroups).

Still in VF after 3 shocks and an antiarrhythmic: at minimum switch pad position to anterior–posterior (vector change) — it's free and has trial data. Double sequential external defibrillation (DSED) "may be considered"; DOSE-VF benefit was concentrated in incessant (not recurrent) VF and lost significance in the as-treated analysis.

body.text: The leader's real job — diagnose the arrest (H's & T's)

While CPR runs, work the reversible causes. H's: Hypovolaemia (fluid/blood), Hypoxia (confirm the tube, check EtCO₂), Hydrogen ion / acidosis, Hypo-/hyperkalaemia (point-of-care K⁺, empiric calcium if suspected), Hypothermia (check the temperature). T's: Tension pneumothorax (finger/needle thoracostomy), Tamponade (bedside echo), Toxins (lipid emulsion, specific antidotes), Thrombosis-coronary (toward the cath lab), Thrombosis-pulmonary (thrombolysis, consider ECPR). Fast POCUS during pulse checks — or TEE if available — is the quickest way to narrow the list in real time.

items: Announce leadership. Clear the room, assign roles by name; extras rotate compressions or become runners.
CPR quality: 100–120/min, 5–6 cm, full recoil, swap q2min, CCF ≥ 60%.
Rhythm check q2min: shockable → shock → resume CPR immediately.
Epi 1 mg q3–5min: early for PEA/asystole, after failed shocks for VF.
Amiodarone or lidocaine for refractory VF/pVT, early.
Calcium / bicarbonate only for a specific indication.
Refractory VF: change pad vector to A–P; consider DSED.
Think H's & T's; POCUS during pulse checks.
Closed-loop everything — if it wasn't repeated back, it wasn't heard.
